area: Area V. Air Traffic Control Clearances and Procedures
objective: By the end of this lesson you can describe pilot and controller responsibilities from the tower through en route control, including clearance void times; teach a learner to copy a clearance with C-R-A-F-T and shorthand, judge whether it can be flown, read it back in standard phraseology, question anything unclear and set the radios to match; and run clearance-copying drills and simulated ATC that build those habits.
why: No one may fly IFR in controlled airspace without an appropriate ATC clearance [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]], and a clearance never authorizes breaking a rule or going below a minimum altitude [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]]. In one IPH case a crew cleared to 7,000 read back 5,000, heard no correction and descended toward the mountains until the GPWS and the controller warned them [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]. Poor radio communication skills have also caused runway incursions [[15:16|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.1]]. Your job is to build a closed loop in every learner: copy it, check it, say it back, ask, and set it up.

warmup: Think first: your instrument learner copies clearances perfectly when you read them slowly at the desk. In the airplane at a busy airport he asks for "say again" three times and still writes 5,000 after the controller said "maintain three thousand, expect five thousand one zero minutes after departure." Is this a knowledge problem, a memory problem or an expectation problem, and how would you build the next lesson?

key_terms.def: An authorization by ATC, to prevent collision between known aircraft, for an aircraft to proceed under specified traffic conditions within controlled airspace [[34:303|P/CG A-6]]. Not authorization to deviate from any rule, regulation or minimum altitude [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].
Directives from ATC requiring a pilot to take a specific action, such as "turn left heading two five zero" or "go around" [[34:314|P/CG A-17]].
The fix, point or location to which an aircraft is cleared [[34:325|P/CG C-4]]; before departure normally the airport of intended landing, stated with the word "airport" [[33:275|AIM 4-4-3]].
Cleared along the route filed in the flight plan; it does not include the altitude, DP or DP transition [[34:325|P/CG C-4]].

key_terms.term: Clearance void if not off by (time)
key_terms.def: The departure release is automatically canceled if takeoff is not made before that time; the IFR flight plan is not canceled [[34:325|P/CG C-4]].
ATC delays a departure for traffic management; the IFR departure clearance is not valid until a release time or more instructions are received [[34:357|P/CG H-2]].
A departure time restriction ATC issues to separate a departing aircraft from other traffic [[34:404|P/CG R-5]]; it is the earliest time the aircraft may depart [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]].
Control of IFR en route traffic within delegated airspace between two or more adjacent approach control facilities, to expedite traffic and reduce communication [[34:430|P/CG T-7]].
An altitude ATC gives for use if two-way communications fail and to help the pilot plan [[34:342|P/CG E-3]]; the pilot keeps the altitude ATC said to maintain [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]].
"Repeat my message back to me" [[34:404|P/CG R-5]]. Airborne pilots should read back altitude assignments, vectors and runway assignments as a double check [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]].
I have received your message, understand it, and will comply with it [[34:445|P/CG W-2]].
Inability to comply with a specific instruction, request or clearance [[34:436|P/CG U-1]].

chunks.title: What this Task asks of an instrument instructor

body.p: This is an all-knowledge Task: the PTS asks you to exhibit instructional knowledge of ATC clearances by describing six elements [[FAA-S-8081-9E:31|PTS V.A]]. "Instructional knowledge" means your explanations follow the methods of the Aviation Instructor's Handbook, including scenario-based lessons [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]]. The Instrument lesson IR.III.A covers the pilot's side of copying and flying a clearance; this lesson adds how you teach it, drill it and play the controller. Flying departures, routes and arrivals is Task V.B, and lost communications is FII.IX.A.

**The legal anchor.** No person may operate an aircraft in controlled airspace under IFR without filing an IFR flight plan and receiving an appropriate ATC clearance [[60:471|14 CFR 91.173]]. A clearance is based on known traffic and known airport conditions. It is not authorization to deviate from any rule, regulation or minimum altitude, or to operate unsafely [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.123: once a clearance is obtained, the pilot in command may not deviate from it unless an amended clearance is obtained, an emergency exists, or the deviation responds to a TCAS resolution advisory. A pilot who is uncertain of a clearance shall immediately request clarification from ATC [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. Except in an emergency, no one may operate contrary to an ATC instruction where ATC is exercised [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]].

body.p: Where it fits in a syllabus: the IFH lesson guide puts ATC clearances in the ground training of Lesson 8, with departure procedures and en route charts, and lists radio communications in the flight training of almost every lesson [[23:343|IFH B-2]]. When possible, each lesson should include radio communications so the learner meets the whole IFR experience on every flight [[23:342|IFH B-1]].

check.q: An examiner asks why a clearance that takes your learner below the MEA does not make the descent legal. What do you answer?
check.a: A clearance is not authorization to deviate from any rule, regulation or minimum altitude; if a clearance would cause that, it is the pilot's responsibility to request an amended clearance [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].

chunks.title: Who does what: pilot and controller responsibilities

body.p: Pilot duties are in the CFRs and controller duties in FAA Order JO 7110.65. The two intentionally overlap, so that if one fails the other can often make up for it [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]]. The pilot in command is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(a)]]. The controller gives first priority to separating aircraft and issuing radar safety alerts, second to other required services, and third to additional services as able [[34:2|AIM 5-5-1]].

head: Item
Pilot
Controller
rows: Air traffic clearance

Acknowledges receipt and understanding; reads back hold short instructions; asks for clarification or amendment when a clearance is not fully understood or is unacceptable for safety; complies promptly [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]]

Issues appropriate clearances; assigns IFR altitudes at or above the minimum IFR altitudes; makes sure the pilot acknowledges; corrects readbacks that are wrong, distorted or incomplete [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]] [[34:3|AIM 5-5-2]]
Vectors
Promptly complies with assigned headings and altitudes; questions any believed to be incorrect [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]]
Vectors IFR aircraft at or above minimum vectoring altitudes, except where specifically authorized [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]]
Safety alert
Takes appropriate action; knows the service is not always available [[34:5|AIM 5-5-7]]
Issues a safety alert when aware of unsafe proximity to terrain, obstructions or another aircraft [[34:5|AIM 5-5-7]]
See and avoid
When conditions permit, sees and avoids traffic, terrain and obstacles, whatever the flight plan [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]]
Gives radar traffic information outside positive control airspace, workload permitting [[34:6|AIM 5-5-8]]
Speed adjustments
Complies unless the safe minimum or maximum speed prevents it, then advises ATC; holds the speed within plus or minus 10 knots [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]]
Assigns speeds when necessary, but not as a substitute for good vectoring [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]]

body.p: Use the MVA chart to teach the altitude side. Terminal controllers can assign altitudes lower than published procedural altitudes, called minimum vectoring altitudes; they are not published for pilots. When an assigned altitude seems too low, query the controller before descending [[23:57|IFH 2-6]].

callout.text: In VMC an IFR clearance does not keep the learner away from VFR traffic. Traffic clearances give standard separation only between IFR flights, and when weather permits, avoiding other aircraft is the pilot's direct responsibility [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].

body.p: Emergency authority closes the loop. In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action the pilot in command may deviate from any rule of Part 91 to the extent required [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]], must tell ATC about a clearance deviation as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]] and, the AIM adds, must also obtain an amended clearance [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]].

check.q: Your learner says, "Radar has us, so terrain is ATC's problem." Using the AIM, how do you correct the idea?
check.a: The controller vectors IFR aircraft at or above minimum vectoring altitudes [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]] and issues safety alerts when aware, but that service is not always available [[34:5|AIM 5-5-7]]. The pilot must still question any assigned altitude believed to be incorrect [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]].

body.p: Towers provide a safe, orderly and expeditious flow of traffic on and near the airport and, when the responsibility is delegated, separate IFR aircraft in the terminal area [[33:204|AIM 4-1-2]]. The tower authorizes aircraft to land, take off or transit the Class D airspace regardless of flight plan or weather [[34:430|P/CG T-7]].

head: Tower position or step
What it means for an IFR flight
rows: Clearance delivery

Its frequency is in the A/FD, now the Chart Supplement, and on the approach chart for the departure airport; where there is no clearance delivery position, ground control does the job [[23:56|IFH 2-5]] [[29:60|IPH 1-44]]
Before engine start
IFR pilots call ground or clearance delivery for engine start time, taxi and clearance information [[33:344|AIM 5-2-4]]
Local controller

Responsible for the Class D airspace and the active runways; at IFR towers it has vectoring authority, at VFR towers it accepts inbound IFR flights from the radar facility and cannot vector [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]
Release
When the pilot accepts the clearance and reports ready, the tower asks the TRACON for a release, and no takeoff clearance comes until the departure controller issues it [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]
Takeoff direction
Where there is airport traffic control service, the controller specifies direction of takeoff, turn or initial heading when necessary, consistent with published DPs or DVAs [[34:9|AIM 5-5-14]]

body.p: Two tower habits to teach. If the learner reports "ready to copy" before the flight strip arrives, ATC answers "clearance on request" and calls back, so the time can be used for taxi and checks [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]. And waiting is normal: an aircraft is not cleared for takeoff until the departure controller can fit it into the flow, so a pilot may have to hold for release [[23:57|IFH 2-6]].

**Line up and wait is not a takeoff clearance.** FAA reviews found that a significant number of pilots read back LUAW correctly and then departed without a takeoff clearance [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]]. If no takeoff clearance comes within a reasonable time, contact ATC [[33:344|AIM 5-2-5]]; in the events studied, two minutes or more passed between the LUAW instruction and the event [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5]].

callout.text: Expectation bias often occurs on the ground while taxiing: pilots perceive the clearance they expect instead of the one given [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Application: have the learner trace every taxi instruction on the airport diagram before he reads it back, even at the home field.

check.q: Your learner is number one at the hold line, called ready, and asks why the tower has not cleared him yet. What do you explain?
check.a: After the pilot reports ready, the tower asks the TRACON for a release and will not issue a takeoff clearance until the departure controller issues it; the flight may have to hold for release [[23:57|IFH 2-6]].

chunks.title: En route control: Center and tower en route control

body.p: Centers serve aircraft on IFR flight plans in controlled airspace, mainly en route [[33:204|AIM 4-1-1]]. Each ARTCC is divided into sectors with their own discrete frequencies, and the pilot is asked to change frequency from sector to sector [[33:359|AIM 5-3-1]]. Most Center airspace is also split by altitude into high and low sectors, and the same controller can be heard on different frequencies through remote sites [[23:58|IFH 2-7]].
Handoff points are set by Letters of Agreement that are not in any FAA publication for pilots, so it is good practice to mark on the en route chart where handoffs occur [[23:66|IFH 2-15]].

bullets: From an airport without a tower the clearance may say "Upon entering controlled airspace, contact Houston Center on 126.5." The pilot is responsible for terrain clearance until reaching the controller's MVA, and "radar contact" alone does not change that [[23:58|IFH 2-7]].

A controller cannot issue an IFR clearance until the aircraft is above the minimum IFR altitude, unless it is able to climb in VFR conditions. "Leaving (altitude) fly (heading) or proceed direct when able" keeps terrain and obstruction responsibility in the flight deck until above the minimum IFR altitude [[23:61|IFH 2-10]].
WHEN ABLE lets the pilot delay compliance until a condition is met, but unlike pilot's discretion the pilot is expected to take the first opportunity to comply [[34:444|P/CG W-1]].
A pilot who departs VFR and accepts a clearance below the MEA, MIA, MVA or OROCA is responsible for terrain and obstruction clearance until reaching it [[33:280|AIM 4-4-9]].

body.p: **Tower en route control (TEC).** TEC links approach control areas with routes from the existing airway structure. The expanded program is generally for nonturbojet aircraft at and below 10,000 feet, entirely within approach control airspace [[33:220|AIM 4-1-19]]. Flights of two hours or less are encouraged, and the pilot requests it by putting "TEC" in the flight plan remarks [[33:221|AIM 4-1-19]]. Route descriptions are in the Chart Supplement; the graphic is not for navigation or detailed planning because not all city pairs are shown [[29:70|IPH 2-10]].

callout.text: Tower: the runways and the Class D [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]. TRACON: the terminal area, sector by sector [[23:57|IFH 2-6]]. Center: en route sectors, high and low [[23:58|IFH 2-7]]. TEC: a short IFR trip that stays in approach control airspace [[33:220|AIM 4-1-19]].

check.q: Departing a nontowered airport, your learner hears "radar contact" from Center while still below the MVA and relaxes about terrain. What do you teach?
check.a: Pilots are responsible for terrain clearance until reaching the controller's MVA; hearing "radar contact" does not relieve them of it [[23:58|IFH 2-7]].

chunks.title: Clearance void times, hold for release and release times

body.p: ATC uses departure restrictions, void times, hold for release and release times to separate departures from other traffic or to regulate the flow. Every departure from an airport without an operating control tower gets either a departure release, with a release and/or void time if needed, or a hold for release [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].

head: Wording
What it means
What the pilot does
rows: "Clearance void if not off by (time)"
The departure release is automatically canceled if takeoff is not made before that time [[34:325|P/CG C-4]]. Airborne at exactly the void time means the clearance is void [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]
Not off? Advise ATC of intentions as soon as possible, within the time ATC gives, which cannot exceed 30 minutes [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]]
"Hold for release"
The IFR departure clearance is not valid until a release time or more instructions are received [[34:357|P/CG H-2]]
May still depart VFR: cancel IFR first and use a VFR code. An IFR clearance may not be available later [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]
"Released for departure at (time)"
The earliest time the aircraft may depart [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]
Do not take off before it [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]
EDCT
The runway release time assigned in a traffic management program [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]
Depart no earlier than 5 minutes before and no later than 5 minutes after it [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]]

callout.text: No contact with ATC within 30 minutes after the void time and the aircraft is considered overdue: search and rescue procedures start. Meanwhile other IFR traffic for that airport is suspended until the pilot calls or 30 minutes pass [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].

body.p: What an expired void time does and does not do: it does not cancel the departure clearance or the IFR flight plan; it withdraws the authority to depart IFR until ATC issues a new release and the pilot acknowledges it [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]]. A pilot who departs at or after the void time has no IFR separation and may be in violation of 91.173, and a pilot who goes VFR instead should not use the old IFR code [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]].

How the learner gets one: the Chart Supplement gives the frequency or phone number for clearance delivery, and on initial contact he says the flight is IFR and names the departure and destination airports [[33:344|AIM 5-2-3]]. A clearance by phone through Flight Service typically includes a void time [[29:59|IPH 1-43]]; other routes are an RCO, a UNICOM operator who relays it, or a GCO, where four key clicks reach ATC and six reach flight service [[29:60|IPH 1-44]]. A clearance relayed by someone other than a controller starts with "ATC clears" [[33:275|AIM 4-4-2]]. If two-way radio contact with the controlling facility is available, get the clearance before becoming airborne when practical [[33:348|AIM 5-2-7]].

callout.text: Teach the learner to help the controller by saying how soon he expects to be airborne, and that a specific void time may be requested when filing [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. Application: brief the call for after the run-up and before-takeoff checklist, so the void time hurries the takeoff, never the checklist.

check.q: Your learner's clearance is void if not off by 1415, and he is still in the run-up at 1413. What does he do?
check.a: He does not rush the takeoff: he must be airborne before the void time [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. He advises ATC of his intentions as soon as possible, within the time ATC gave and never more than 30 minutes after the void time [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].

chunks.title: Copying a clearance: C-R-A-F-T, shorthand and timing

body.p: Clearances follow a format: clearance limit, route including any departure procedure, initial altitude, departure frequency and transponder code. Except for the transponder code, the pilot knows most of these before engine start, and one technique is writing C-R-A-F-T [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. The AIM lists what a clearance normally contains as the clearance limit, departure procedure, route of flight, altitude data and holding instructions [[33:275|AIM 4-4-3]] [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]. When conducting an IFR operation, make a written record of the clearance: it may differ from the flight plan, and ATC may add conditions because other aircraft are involved [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]].

head: Letter
Item
What to teach about it
rows: C
Clearance limit
Normally the airport of intended landing, said with the word "airport", because many airports and NAVAIDs share a name [[33:275|AIM 4-4-3]]
R
Route

Normally the filed route, but ATC frequently has to change it [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]. "Cleared as filed" does not include the altitude, DP or DP transition [[34:325|P/CG C-4]]; a DP's name, number and transition are stated before "then as filed" [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]]

Altitude
Normally "maintain"; when it differs from the request, ATC tells when to expect a change if possible [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]
F
Frequency
Departure control; it may be omitted when it is printed on the assigned DP [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8]]
T
Transponder
The code is generated by computer and can seldom be known in advance [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]

body.p: **The IFH method.** Monitor clearance delivery to learn which departure procedure other flights are getting, pre-write the expected items next to C-R-A-F-T, then call "ready to copy." As the controller reads, check each item against the notes; draw a line through anything that changed and write in the new item [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

**Shorthand.** The FAA recommends the Appendix A system, but applicants may use any shorthand, in any language, that ensures accurate compliance; no system is required by regulation, and practicing one lets a pilot copy long clearances as fast as they are read [[23:340|IFH A-1]]. Example (in the figure): "CAF M→ RH RV V18 ↑40 SQ 0700 DPC 120.4" is cleared as filed, maintain runway heading for radar vector to Victor 18, climb to 4,000, squawk 0700, departure control 120.4 [[23:340|IFH A-1]]. The M with an arrow through it is the symbol for maintain, a plain M means magnetic, and the up arrow means climb to, with the altitude in hundreds of feet [[23:340|IFH A-1]] [[23:341|IFH A-2]]. Pilots should develop a set method for copying taxi clearances too [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.4]].

**Timely.** File at least 30 minutes before the estimated departure time to avoid delay in getting a clearance [[23:293|IFH 10-2]]; flight strips reach the tower about 30 minutes before the proposed departure time [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. Where a pre-taxi clearance program exists, call clearance delivery or ground no more than 10 minutes before proposed taxi time [[33:343|AIM 5-2-1]]. For the IFR part of a VFR/IFR flight, request the clearance before the fix where IFR begins, in time to avoid delay [[33:347|AIM 5-2-6]].

callout.text: C-R-A-F-T: Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency, Transponder [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. Pre-write, listen, cross out, read back.

check.q: Your learner asks why he should write anything before calling, since the clearance will be read to him anyway. What do you say?
check.a: He knows most items before engine start. Pre-writing them means he only checks them and replaces what changed, so most of the clearance is already copied before he keys the microphone [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].

chunks.title: Teaching clearance copying: memory, drills and progression

body.p: Explain why the pencil matters. Short-term memory holds information for roughly 30 seconds and usually about seven chunks. Coding information takes 5 to 10 seconds, and if the coding is interrupted the information is easily lost [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. Application: count the items of a real clearance with the learner; with a frequency and a four-digit code it is well past seven, and the next radio call is the interruption.

The AIH's own remedy is coding: rehearsal and sorting information into systematic chunks help retention in short-term memory [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. C-R-A-F-T gives the learner five fixed boxes to sort each item into. Notepads and heading bugs are reminders the AIH names for information that would otherwise have to be held in memory [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

Example clearance drill (instructor's choice)

Recite C-R-A-F-T and the common shorthand symbols

Put two or more concepts together and explain them [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]
Explain why "as filed" carries no altitude [[34:325|P/CG C-4]]

Perform consistently after practice [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Copy and read back a full clearance at normal speed

Associate it with other blocks of learning; the objective of aviation instruction [[25:66|AIH 3-15]]
Brief the lost-communication route and altitude from the clearance just copied [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185(c)(1)]] [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]

body.p: Drill and practice rests on the law of exercise: connections are strengthened with practice, and the mind rarely retains a new practice after one exposure [[25:125|AIH 5-22]]. Retrieval depends on frequency and recency of use; knowledge that was used recently but not often is especially easy to forget and needs regular rehearsal [[25:88|AIH 3-37]].

callout.text: Application: a progression that works. (1) At the desk, read printed clearances slowly, then at normal speed. (2) Have the learner copy clearances given to other flights while monitoring clearance delivery, which the IFH recommends anyway [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. (3) In an ATD or the parked airplane: copy, read back, set the radios. (4) In the airplane: the real clearance, with you taking the pencil only if he falls behind.

check.q: Your learner recites the shorthand list perfectly but drops the squawk code every time a clearance is read at normal speed. Which learning level has he reached, and what do you change?
check.a: Rote: he can repeat what was taught [[25:65|AIH 3-14]]. Move him to practice at normal speed with C-R-A-F-T as his chunks, since sorting into chunks helps short-term retention [[25:87|AIH 3-36]] and practice strengthens the connections [[25:125|AIH 5-22]].

chunks.title: Ability to comply: can we fly what we accept?

body.p: It is the pilot's responsibility to accept or refuse a clearance [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]. Once accepted, it is flown: pilots are expected to execute a clearance on receipt, and an added restriction does not authorize deviating from the route or any other provision [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]. Before accepting, the pilot should know where the named navigation facilities are, plus the route and point-to-point times [[23:295|IFH 10-4]].

head: Check before accepting
What the sources say
rows: Can the radios receive what the clearance uses?
Notify ATC immediately if the equipment cannot receive the signals needed to comply [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]
Is the DP in hand and flyable?

Using a DP requires at least its textual description; a pilot who does not want one says so or files "NO DP"; once accepted, comply [[23:296|IFH 10-5]]. Contact ATC if unable to meet the climb gradient [[29:59|IPH 1-43]]
Can the airplane climb as expected?
Optimum rate to 1,000 feet from the assigned altitude, then 500 to 1,500 fpm; advise ATC if unable to make at least 500 fpm [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]
Is the assigned speed safe?
Pilots may refuse speed adjustments they consider excessive or contrary to the aircraft's operating specifications [[34:6|AIM 5-5-9]]
Is RNAV working?
If unable to comply with an RNAV or RNP procedure, advise ATC, for example "unable RNAV, request amended clearance" [[34:10|AIM 5-5-16]]

body.p: Pilots may request a different clearance when they have information that makes another course of action more practicable, or when equipment limitations or company procedures forbid compliance [[33:277|AIM 4-4-4]]. Assigned headings are started promptly, completed and held [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]. Even "cleared for immediate takeoff" may be refused if, in the pilot's opinion, compliance would adversely affect the operation [[33:285|AIM 4-4-13]].

callout.text: ATC should be advised immediately if there is any uncertainty about the ability to comply with any of their instructions [[33:345|AIM 5-2-5]]. Teach "unable" as a professional word: it simply indicates inability to comply with a specific instruction, request or clearance [[34:436|P/CG U-1]].
Application: before every readback in training, have the learner ask himself aloud, "Can this airplane, these avionics and I do this?" It turns K3 into a habit instead of a lecture.

check.q: Heavily loaded on a hot day, your learner is cleared to climb and can manage only 300 fpm. What does he do?
check.a: Tell ATC: a pilot unable to climb at least 500 fpm advises ATC [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]], and may request a different clearance because of aircraft limitations [[33:277|AIM 4-4-4]].

body.p: Airborne pilots should read back the parts of clearances and instructions that contain altitude assignments, vectors or runway assignments. Reading back the numbers is a double check that catches numbers misheard or given wrong [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]]. The IFH also recommends reading the IFR clearance back to clearance delivery [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]. ATC uses standard phraseology and requires readbacks to verify understanding, and to complete the loop the controller must also clearly understand the pilot's readback [[23:294|IFH 10-3]] [[23:295|IFH 10-4]].

**Correct and timely.** Acknowledge all callups and clearances unless the controller says otherwise, with the call sign at the beginning or end [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]]. Application: read back promptly and from what was written, because short-term memory holds information for only about 30 seconds [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]. The AIM's rules for a correct readback:

bullets: Include the aircraft identification in all readbacks and acknowledgments [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]]; it matters more as the frequency gets busy and when similar call signs are on it [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].
Read back altitudes, altitude restrictions and vectors in the same sequence as given [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].
Do not read back altitudes from charted procedures unless the controller states them [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].
The initial readback of a taxi, departure or landing clearance includes the runway, with left, right or center [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].
Read back hold short instructions [[34:2|AIM 5-5-2]]; the IPH recommends reading back in full all clearances involving holding short, line up and wait and crossing runways [[29:22|IPH 1-6]].
Acknowledge frequency changes. A pilot who just switches leaves the controller unable to tell whether the instruction was received or the radio failed [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].

head: Word (P/CG)
Meaning
rows: Roger
I have received all of your last transmission. Not an answer to a yes or no question [[34:407|P/CG R-8]]
Wilco
Received, understood, and will comply [[34:445|P/CG W-2]]
Affirmative / Negative
Yes / "No," "permission not granted" or "that is not correct" [[34:302|P/CG A-5]] [[34:385|P/CG N-2]]
Say again
Request to repeat the last transmission [[34:413|P/CG S-2]]
Verify
Request confirmation of information [[34:438|P/CG V-1]]
Unable
Cannot comply with a specific instruction, request or clearance [[34:436|P/CG U-1]]
Stand by
Pause; it is not an approval or a denial [[34:420|P/CG S-9]]

body.p: **Numbers.** Below 18,000 feet say the separate digits of the thousands plus the hundreds, as in "one two thousand five hundred"; at and above FL 180 say "flight level" and the digits [[33:233|AIM 4-2-9]]. Frequencies use "point" [[33:233|AIM 4-2-8]], and a heading is three digits, as in "heading one zero zero" [[33:234|AIM 4-2-10]]. On initial contact with an ATC facility, report the exact altitude to the nearest 100 feet [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]]; in a radar environment, also give the assigned altitude with "level," "climbing to" or "descending to" [[33:374|AIM 5-3-1]]. For a radar departure the IPH says the same: call sign, the altitude you are climbing through and the altitude you are climbing to [[29:54|IPH 1-38]]. The IFH sample call, "Birmingham Departure Cessna 1230A climbing through 2,700 heading 240," gives the present altitude so the controller can check the encoded altitude, but leaves out the assigned 4,000 [[23:323|IFH 10-32]]; teach the AIM and IPH form.

callout.text: When ATC answers a report with "roger," it only means ATC received the transmission, not that it understood it. In the IPH case a corporate crew reported leaving FL 310 to make an "expect" crossing altitude, heard "roger," and had no clearance to descend [[29:110|IPH 2-50]] [[29:111|IPH 2-51]].

check.q: ATC says, "Cessna 5432K, turn right heading 090, descend and maintain 4,000." What is the correct readback?
check.a: "Right heading zero niner zero, descend and maintain four thousand, Cessna 5432K": the vector and the altitude in the order given, with the call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

chunks.title: Interpreting a clearance and asking for clarification, verification or change

body.p: The rule is short: a pilot who is uncertain of a clearance shall immediately request clarification from ATC [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]. The AIM asks pilots to request verification or clarification if ANY portion of the clearance is not clearly understood [[33:347|AIM 5-2-6]]. If necessary, use plain English and expect the controller to answer the same way [[23:55|IFH 2-4]]; when concise phraseology is not enough, use whatever words are necessary [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]].

head: Clearance wording
Correct interpretation
rows: "Cleared to (destination) airport as filed"
The filed route only: no altitude, DP or DP transition [[34:325|P/CG C-4]]
"Maintain 3,000, expect 5,000 ten minutes after departure"

Fly 3,000. The expect altitude is for communication failure and planning [[34:342|P/CG E-3]]: after a radio failure in IFR conditions the pilot flies the highest of the last assigned altitude, the minimum IFR altitude and the expected altitude [[60:483|14 CFR 91.185(c)(2)]]; charted "expect" altitudes, too, are for planning and are not crossing restrictions until ATC issues them [[29:111|IPH 2-51]]
"Descend at pilot's discretion, maintain 6,000"
Start when you wish, at any rate, level off as desired, but never return to an altitude once vacated [[33:280|AIM 4-4-10]]
"Cruise 5,000"
Any altitude from the minimum IFR altitude up to 5,000; after reporting leaving an altitude in the block, the pilot may not return to it without clearance [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]]
A new "climb and maintain" that leaves out an earlier crossing restriction
The last clearance has precedence: omitted altitude restrictions are canceled, including DP and STAR restrictions [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]]
"Descend and maintain (altitude); then, reduce speed to (speed)"
The order of delivery, with "then" between, is the order of execution [[33:283|AIM 4-4-12]]

body.p: Use the IPH holding figure to show how much a clearance can leave to the chart: a charted hold needs at least the direction to hold, the fix and an EFC time, while an uncharted hold adds the holding course, the outbound leg length and any nonstandard turns [[29:110|IPH 2-50]]. If there is no charted hold and no instructions have come, ask ATC for holding instructions before reaching the fix [[33:276|AIM 4-4-3]].
**Clarification, verification or change: the words to use.**

bullets: Not sure the clearance was for you: "VERIFY CLEARANCE FOR (your complete call sign)" [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].
Did not hear it all: "say again," a request to repeat the last transmission [[34:413|P/CG S-2]].

ATC says "verify assigned altitude as (altitude)": confirm it if it is correct, or give the actual or different assigned altitude. Do not change altitude to the one in the request unless the controller authorizes it [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1]].
Flight plan changed after filing: state the change on the initial call and request a full route clearance [[33:347|AIM 5-2-6]].
Clearance would break a rule or put the aircraft in jeopardy: it is the pilot's responsibility to request an amended clearance [[33:275|AIM 4-4-1]].
Heading or altitude seems wrong: question it [[34:5|AIM 5-5-6]].

callout.text: Unless ATC authorizes it, no person may operate according to a clearance or instruction issued to another aircraft for radar air traffic control purposes [[60:451|14 CFR 91.123(e)]].

check.q: ATC asks your learner to "verify assigned altitude." He answers "roger." What is wrong, and what should he say?
check.a: VERIFY is a request for confirmation [[34:438|P/CG V-1]], and "roger" only says the transmission was received; it should not answer a question that needs a yes or no [[34:407|P/CG R-8]]. He should confirm that the assigned altitude is correct as stated, or tell the controller his different assigned altitude, with his call sign [[33:375|AIM 5-3-1]].

chunks.title: Setting communication and navigation frequencies to match the clearance

body.p: Communication and navigation aids should be set up before taxi: setting radios while rolling is the leading cause of heads-down time and hurts see and avoid [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.3]]. In the IFH sample flight the pilot reads back the clearance, reviews the DP, finds the departure frequency printed on it, tunes the frequencies and sets up navigation for the departure, and only then calls ground [[23:322|IFH 10-31]].

head: Radio
What the clearance drives
rows: COM
ATC uses 118.000 to 136.975 MHz; if ATC assigns a frequency the radio cannot select, ask for another [[23:53|IFH 2-2]]. Do not change to departure control until requested [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8]]
NAV
VORs use 108.0 to 117.95 MHz; the only positive identification is the Morse code or the recorded voice ID that ends in "VOR" [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]]
GPS

Enter the planned flight before departure [[23:322|IFH 10-31]]. The AIM tells FMS users who get a change of runway, transition or procedure on an assigned RNAV DP or STAR to verify the changes are loaded [[34:11|AIM 5-5-16]]
Transponder
ATC assigns the code [[23:54|IFH 2-3]] and gives it before takeoff when appropriate [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8]]; it is good practice to confirm code changes and idents aloud [[23:54|IFH 2-3]]
Audio panel
Selects receivers and transmitter [[23:53|IFH 2-2]], so the pilot can listen to ATIS on one receiver while talking to ATC on the other, or monitor a NAV receiver's identifier [[23:54|IFH 2-3]]

body.p: In flight, select a new frequency as soon as possible unless told to change at a time, fix or altitude; in that case monitor the current frequency until reaching it [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]]. During maintenance a VOR may send a T-E-S-T code or no identifier, and equipment that decodes the identifier makes listening unnecessary [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]].

Teach purpose before buttons. Beginning instrument learners commonly make errors managing two COM radios with active and standby frequencies, and error rates often drop quickly once they understand each radio's purpose, such as ATIS, ground and tower [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]. Have as many frequencies as possible written down before they are needed [[23:64|IFH 2-13]].

callout.text: Application: give each radio a job for the whole flight and brief it, for example COM1 for ATC, COM2 for ATIS and the next facility, NAV1 for the cleared course and NAV2 to cross-check fixes. Then every clearance item has a home before it is spoken. The IFH sample flight does the same when it tunes the VORTAC and sets the course as a backup to the GPS approach [[23:324|IFH 10-33]].

check.q: Your learner's clearance has no departure frequency. Where does he find it, and when does he switch?
check.a: Controllers may omit it when it is published on the assigned DP, and pilots should not change to departure control until requested [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8]]. In the IFH flight the pilot found 123.8 on the DP and switched when the tower said "contact departure" [[23:322|IFH 10-31]] [[23:323|IFH 10-32]].

chunks.title: Risk: where the clearance loop breaks

body.p: The RMH lists unexpected ATC clearances, restrictions or reroutes, controller errors, radio congestion and communication failure among common threats [[30:44|RMH 6-1]]. The defense is clear communication: agree on the plan of action, ask for clarification and question any inconsistency [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

head: Failure
What happened in the sources
What you teach
rows: Wrong readback not caught
An MD-80 crew cleared to 7,000 read back 5,000, got no correction and descended until GPWS and controller warnings [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]
The readback is a double check on the numbers [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]], but silence is not proof. Read back from the paper, not from memory
Words that sound alike
A crew read back "leaving 5,000" for what was probably "reaching 5,000," climbed, and ended with inadequate separation; the two words sound much alike [[29:109|IPH 2-49]]
When the timing word is unclear, ask at once [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]]
Expectation bias
Pilots perceive the clearance they expect instead of the one given, especially routine taxi routes [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]
Pre-write the expected items, but cross them out the moment a change is heard [[23:56|IFH 2-5]]
Similar call signs
An aircraft at the top of a holding stack acknowledges an approach clearance meant for the one at the bottom [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]]
Full call sign, and "verify clearance for" when in doubt [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]]
"Expect" taken as a clearance
A crew descended for an "expect" crossing altitude and had no clearance [[29:110|IPH 2-50]] [[29:111|IPH 2-51]]
Expect altitudes are for planning until ATC issues them [[29:111|IPH 2-51]]
Hurry
The more hurried the work, the more slips [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]
Take time: working deliberately at a comfortable pace reduces errors [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]

body.p: Use the AIH's words in the debrief. A slip is planning one thing and doing another, like turning for runway 30 out of habit after being assigned runway 12; a mistake is a plan that is wrong, often from a gap or misconception in understanding [[25:84|AIH 3-33]]. Some errors are slips that simply show a need for more practice; others point to methods or habits that can be improved [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

callout.text: Fatigue stops pilots from taking extra steps to verify what they think is happening and makes expectation and confirmation bias more likely [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Application: put the hardest clearance drills early in a lesson, not at the end of a long day.

check.q: Your learner reads back 5,000 when you are fairly sure the controller said 7,000, and the controller says nothing. What do you teach right there?
check.a: Controllers should correct a wrong readback [[34:3|AIM 5-5-2]], but the IPH case shows one can go uncorrected [[29:121|IPH 3-9]]. A pilot who is uncertain immediately requests clarification [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(a)]].

chunks.title: Simulating ATC: role play, scripted clearances and the training device

body.p: The AIH gives you the tools. In role playing the learner gets a general description of a situation and applies new knowledge in a role [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]; simulation and role-play put the learner into a real-world scenario and promote critical thinking [[25:123|AIH 5-20]]. In clearance training you play the controller and the learner plays himself.

head: Telling-and-doing step
The clearance version
rows: Instructor tells, instructor does
You call for a clearance aloud, copy it in C-R-A-F-T, read it back and set the radios, explaining as you go; the demonstration follows the order of the explanation [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner tells you what to write, read back and set while you do it. He can organize the steps, and you see his understanding before he is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner tells, learner does
He copies, reads back and sets the radios while thinking aloud, so you can tell a misconception from a lack of skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner does, instructor evaluates
A cold clearance with a change in it; assess each element, not only the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]

body.p: Where to simulate: an integrated curriculum can use an FFS, FTD or ATD for procedural training after the knowledge is taught, then move to the airplane to verify proficiency [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. In scenario visualization the instructor adds unforeseen changes, and radio outages are the AIH's example for instrument airplane learners [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. A visit to an ATC facility shows learners the NAS from another perspective [[25:172|AIH 9-2]], but visits may not always be approved, so request one early [[33:204|AIM 4-1-6]] [[33:205|AIM 4-1-6]].
Application: script your simulated clearances so each one tests a rule from this lesson:

bullets: A changed route, so pre-written items must be crossed out [[23:56|IFH 2-5]].
An "expect" altitude next to the assigned one [[34:342|P/CG E-3]].
A void time that arrives during the run-up [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]].
An amended altitude that leaves out an earlier crossing restriction [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]].
A look-alike call sign on the frequency [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].
A frequency change at a fix [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].
A fast, run-together read, so the learner must ask "say again" [[34:413|P/CG S-2]].

callout.text: Application: in the airplane keep simulated ATC on the intercom and announce it ("simulated clearance") before reading it. Real ATC always wins: except in an emergency, no one may operate contrary to an ATC instruction where ATC is exercised [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(b)]]. The PTS also tells evaluators not to simulate any condition that may jeopardize safe flight [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]].

body.p: Correcting errors in a drill: safety permitting, it is often better to let the learner go part of the way into a mistake and find the way out; learners who seldom correct an error have trouble learning [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]. If he performs correctly but you doubt he understands, vary the scenario or combine it with other operations [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

check.q: In the telling-and-doing technique, why is the "learner tells, instructor does" step valuable for clearance training?
check.a: Freed from doing it, the learner organizes the steps, and you can evaluate his understanding and correct a misunderstanding before he becomes absorbed in controlling the aircraft [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

chunks.title: Common errors and how the examiner tests this Task

body.p: The PTS lists no common errors for this Task [[FAA-S-8081-9E:31|PTS V.A]], so the table gathers the cautions the sources give. Evaluators should test application and correlation with scenario-based questions where possible, and judge whether your descriptions follow AIH teaching methods [[FAA-S-8081-9E:10|PTS Use of the PTS]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. For a flight instructor with an airplane rating adding the instrument rating, Area V is required, and the evaluator selects at least one of its two Tasks [[FAA-S-8081-9E:31|PTS Area V NOTE]] [[FAA-S-8081-9E:18|PTS Addition of an Instrument Rating table]].

head: Error
What you see or hear
Likely cause (instructor's view)
Fix and how you teach it
rows: Expect altitude copied as the assigned one
"50" after A when ATC said maintain 3,000, expect 5,000
Expectation; no separate place for "expect"
Separate symbols for maintain or climb and for expect [[23:340|IFH A-1]] [[23:341|IFH A-2]]; expect is for planning and communication failure [[34:342|P/CG E-3]]
Climbing to the filed altitude after "as filed"
Climbs past the assigned altitude
Belief that "as filed" includes the altitude
"As filed" does not include the en route altitude [[33:346|AIM 5-2-6]]
Readback misses the key number
Long readback, charted altitudes read, assigned altitude missing
Not knowing what must be read back
Altitudes, restrictions, vectors and runway, in order, with call sign; charted altitudes only if stated [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]
Short or missing call sign
"Roger" or "32K" with look-alikes on frequency
Habit
Call sign in every readback and acknowledgment [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]], never abbreviated when similar call signs are on the frequency [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]]
Takeoff at or after the void time
Lifts off at 1415 on a 1415 void time
Time pressure
Airborne before it [[23:56|IFH 2-5]], or call ATC for a new release [[33:347|AIM 5-2-7]]
Early or silent frequency change
Switches to departure on the ground, or switches without a word
Trying to stay ahead
Change only when requested, and acknowledge [[33:349|AIM 5-2-8]] [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]]
Navigating on an unidentified VOR
Needle alive, no identifier heard or decoded
Rushed setup
Identify by Morse code or voice ID [[33:68|AIM 1-1-3]], or by a decoded identifier if the equipment decodes it [[33:69|AIM 1-1-3]]
Accepting what cannot be flown
Cannot make 500 fpm or the DP climb gradient and says nothing
Reluctance to say "unable"
Keeping a canceled restriction
Levels at an old crossing altitude after a new altitude was issued
Not knowing that the last clearance has precedence
Omitted altitude restrictions are canceled [[33:281|AIM 4-4-10]]

body.p: In the flight portion the evaluator acts as a student during selected maneuvers to see you analyze and correct simulated common errors [[FAA-S-8081-9E:14|PTS Evaluator Responsibility]]. Use the same pattern orally here: name the error, give its likely cause, give the fix. The AIH adds: point out errors when they occur, ask the learner to explain why they happened, and let him practice recovering from common errors [[25:86|AIH 3-35]].

check.q: An examiner playing your learner writes "50" after A on hearing "maintain three thousand, expect five thousand one zero minutes after departure." Name the error and your fix.
check.a: He copied the expect altitude as the assigned one. Show the separate shorthand for climb or maintain and for expect [[23:340|IFH A-1]], and explain that an expect altitude is for planning and communication failure [[34:342|P/CG E-3]].
